blocks.text: One MCP server instance can only take so many connections before it runs out of room.
Running several instances behind a load balancer spreads that traffic across a fleet.
This lesson looks at how that balancer picks an instance, and what makes MCP different.
1. What a Load Balancer Does for an MCP Fleet

blocks.alt: A load balancer distributes client connections across three MCP server instances

blocks.text: A load balancer sits in front of a pool of MCP server instances and picks one for each new connection.
Its job has two parts, spread load evenly and avoid sending traffic to an instance that cannot serve it.
Everything in this lesson is really just different ways of doing those two things well.
2. Round Robin, Rotating Through Instances

blocks.alt: Round robin rotates each new request to the next instance in turn

blocks.text: Round robin is the simplest algorithm, each new connection goes to the next instance in the list.
Instance one gets the first connection, instance two the second, then back to instance one again.
This is the default in most load balancers when no other algorithm is configured explicitly.
3. Least Connections, Following Current Load

blocks.alt: Least connections routes a new request to whichever instance has the fewest active connections

blocks.text: Least connections sends each new connection to whichever instance has the fewest active connections right now.
This adapts to reality instead of just taking turns, a busy instance gets skipped over automatically.
For MCP, where sessions can stay open for minutes, this often matches reality better than round robin.
4. Weighted Algorithms for Uneven Instances
Weighted round robin and weighted least connections add a multiplier per instance in the pool.
A bigger instance gets a higher weight and receives proportionally more of the incoming traffic.
5. Picking an Algorithm for Your Fleet
Neither algorithm wins outright, the right pick depends on how uniform your instances and sessions are.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Fits best when","Watch out for"],"rows":[["Round Robin","Instances are identical and sessions are short or similar in cost","Long uneven sessions can pile up on one instance"],["Least Connections","Sessions vary in length or cost, common for MCP","Needs accurate live connection counts to work well"],["Weighted variants","Instances have different capacity","Weights need updating as capacity changes over time"]]}

blocks.title: A quick rule of thumb
blocks.content: If your MCP sessions are long lived and uneven in cost, start with least connections, not round robin.

blocks.text: 6. The Session Affinity Challenge, Unique to MCP

blocks.alt: A client needs to keep landing on the same instance for session affinity

blocks.text: MCP sessions are not stateless one off requests, an instance builds in memory state for each session it owns.
The Distributed MCP Architectures lesson covers this in depth, this lesson focuses on the balancer side of it.
If a session sends its next message to a different instance, that instance has never heard of it.
The balancer needs a way to remember which instance owns a session and keep routing it there.
7. Cookie Based Sticky Sessions
One common fix is a cookie, the balancer sets a cookie naming the instance on the first response.
Every later request from that client carries the cookie back, letting the balancer route it consistently.
This works well for browser based clients, but it depends on the client actually storing and resending it.
8. IP Hash and Session Id Routing

blocks.alt: IP hash routing is compared against session id based routing

blocks.text: IP hash routes based on the client address, the same address always lands on the same instance.
It is simple but blunt, many users sharing one corporate proxy address all pile onto one instance.
Routing by an explicit session id header is more precise, and is what most MCP deployments prefer.
9. Sticky Sessions on Nginx
Nginx does not parse MCP session ids natively, so a common pattern hashes a custom header instead.
The consistent keyword matters, it minimizes how many sessions move when an instance joins or leaves.
10. Sticky Sessions on a Cloud Load Balancer
Managed load balancers offer the same idea through configuration instead of custom hashing logic.
Application based stickiness like this reads a cookie your MCP server sets, giving you control of the key.
11. Health Checks, Active and Passive

blocks.alt: Active health checks are compared against passive health checks

blocks.text: Active health checks are the balancer polling each instance on a schedule, asking if it is still okay.
Passive health checks watch real traffic instead, marking an instance unhealthy after enough failures.
Most production setups use both, active checks catch a dead instance fast, passive checks catch decline.
12. Health Check Based Routing in Action

code.content:
GET /health HTTP/1.1
Host: mcp-instance-2

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"status": "ok", "activeSessions": 84}

blocks.text: When an instance fails its health check, the balancer pulls it out of rotation right away.
New connections stop arriving at it, existing ones are handled per the draining policy below.
13. Draining Connections Before Removal

blocks.alt: An instance drains its open connections before being removed from rotation

blocks.text: Pulling an unhealthy instance out instantly can cut off sessions that were still working fine.
Connection draining gives existing sessions a grace period to finish before full removal.
That delay gives in flight MCP sessions up to two minutes to finish before the instance disappears.
14. Affinity and Health Checks Working Together
Sticky routing and health checks need to cooperate, not conflict, or sessions stick to a dead instance.
A good balancer checks health first, only sending a session back to its sticky instance if it is healthy.
If the sticky instance is down, the session needs a fallback, which is why shared state matters so much.
15. Monitoring a Load Balancer in Production
Watching uptime alone is not enough, connection counts per instance reveal whether load is truly balanced.
A sudden imbalance across instances, or a spike in failed health checks, are early warning signals.

items: Active connections per instance, to catch uneven load early.
Health check failure rate, to catch instances that are flapping.
Request latency per instance, since a slow instance can still look healthy.

blocks.text: 16. A Minimal Production Checklist
Before calling a load balanced MCP fleet production ready, a short checklist is worth walking through.

items: An algorithm, round robin or least connections, is chosen deliberately, not left at a default.
Sticky routing is configured if any instance holds in memory session state.
Both active and passive health checks are enabled against a real health endpoint.
Connection draining is configured so removing an instance never cuts sessions off mid flight.

blocks.text: Worked Example, Routing a Fleet of Five
Picture five MCP instances behind a balancer using least connections with session id stickiness.
A new client connects, the balancer picks instance three, the one with the fewest active connections.
The balancer tags that session with instance three, so its next few requests all land there too.
Instance three then fails its health check, the balancer stops sending it new sessions and drains it.
The client reconnects, finds instance three missing, and is routed fresh to instance one instead.
Because session state was shared, not stuck in memory on instance three, instance one picks up cleanly.
Common Mistakes

items: Using round robin for long, uneven MCP sessions, letting load drift badly out of balance over time.
Enabling sticky sessions without shared or persisted state, so a lost instance loses every session it owned.
Configuring only active health checks and missing the slow, gradual failures that passive checks catch.
Removing an unhealthy instance with no drain time, cutting off sessions that were still working fine.
Setting stickiness once and never revisiting it as the fleet grows or session patterns change.

blocks.text: Practice
Set up nginx locally with two or three backend instances and switch between round robin and least connections.

for i in $(seq 1 6); do
  curl -s http://localhost/mcp/ -H "X-MCP-Session-Id: demo"
done

blocks.text: Watch which instance handles each request, then add the hash directive and watch it stick to one instance.
Key Takeaway
A load balancer for an MCP fleet must do more than rotate traffic, it must respect session state and health.
Round robin and least connections solve distribution, sticky routing and health checks solve reliability, and MCP needs both done well.
